claims.text: Superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the degree of atomic-scale chemical disorder.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder modulates electron scattering.
Changes in electron scattering modify electron-phonon coupling and thereby set the superconducting transition temperature.
The as-cast alloy has a statistically homogeneous elemental distribution and high chemical disorder.
Post-casting heat treatment can promote short-range chemical order and reduce atomic-scale disorder without changing overall composition.
Random elemental distribution creates atomic-scale electron-scattering centers.
High chemical disorder increases electron scattering.
Chemical disorder and its associated scattering can modify the electron-phonon coupling strength and the density of states at the Fermi level.
Altered electron-phonon coupling influences superconducting pairing and therefore Tc.
Partially ordered, heat-treated samples will have a higher Tc than fully disordered as-cast samples.
Partially ordered, heat-treated samples will have lower residual resistivity than fully disordered as-cast samples.
An increase in Tc accompanying lower residual resistivity would indicate reduced scattering-induced suppression of superconductivity.
The as-cast baseline retains maximum chemical disorder.
The proposed mechanism is limited to alloys in which bulk random mixing is the primary source of scattering.
Grain-boundary effects or secondary-phase precipitation may dominate superconducting properties and place the alloy outside the hypothesis's scope.
The magnitudes of changes in Tc and electron-phonon coupling may depend on alloy composition and processing parameters.
Residual resistivity can be used as an indicator of electron scattering.
Failure of heat-treated samples to show a statistically significant increase in Tc and decrease in residual resistivity relative to the as-cast control is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.
